Jet A is moved primarily by pipeline or vessel to terminals and onward to airports by pipeline or truck (Figure 11). SAF coprocessed at an existing refinery or blended into refinery storage is certified per ASTM D1655 and flows through the supply chain in a business-as-usual scenario. SAF produced at a stand-alone facility must be blended somewhere in the supply chain with Jet A—previous reports examined options (Moriarty and McCormick 2024; Moriarty, Milbrandt, and Tao 2021). Fuel quality requirements and establishing SAF as ASTM D1655 certified prior to the airport was the key reason for identifying existing terminals as the best option for blending. Terminals have blending equipment, technology, permits, insurance, and staff knowledge because it is a part of their on-road transportation fuel activities. Blending can occur at the terminal directly linked to an airport or anywhere upstream. Demonstration projects brought SAF blended in Houston up the Colonial Pipeline to Linden, New Jersey, and onward on Buckeye’s pipeline to LaGuardia International Airport in New York and by truck to Patrick Leahy Burlington International Airport (Neste 2022; Business Air News 2025).
